Achieve a Darker Bedroom

Many Treasure Coast homes have large windows and open floor plans, which makes a fully dark bedroom harder to reach at night. Two Hunter Douglas features address this. Duolite gives you a light-filtering shade and a room-darkening shade in one headrail, and LightLock adds side channels that block light at the edges of the window. Together they cover both the center of the window and the gaps around it.

How Duolite and LightLock Block Light

Duolite is a dual-shade design for select Hunter Douglas cellular shades. A light-filtering shade sits in front and a room-darkening shade sits behind it, both on the same headrail. During the day you can lower only the front shade for soft, diffused light. At night you lower the back shade for room darkening. Because the two shades operate independently, you get flexible light control from a single window treatment.

LightLock is a separate option available on select Hunter Douglas shades such as Duette. It is a side channel that runs down each side of the shade and fits close to the window frame. The channel covers the gap where light normally slips past the edge of a shade, which is the most common source of light leakage in a bedroom. LightLock is not a shade line of its own and it is not a roller-shade feature.

Installation matters as much as the product. Precise measuring and a proper outside mount let the side channels sit tight against the frame so the seal works as intended. In the Shade measures each window and installs the system so the light-blocking pieces line up correctly, which is especially helpful on the large windows common in Stuart, Palm City, and Port St. Lucie homes.

Choosing the Right Duette Shade

Selecting the right window treatment means balancing light control with how the room looks and feels. For a bedroom, Duolite gives you both a light-filtering option and a room-darkening option in one unit, so the same window can serve you at different times of day.

Think about how the room is used and how much natural light you want versus how dark you need it for sleep. Large windows often benefit most from the edge coverage that LightLock provides.   2. Determine Desired Level of Darkness: For the darkest bedroom, pair a room-darkening Duette fabric with LightLock side channels. The channels fit close to the window frame and cover the light leaks that standard shades leave behind.
  3. Consider Insulation: The honeycomb cellular design of Duette shades traps air in the pockets, which adds a layer of insulation at the window. That helps moderate the temperature near the glass during hot Treasure Coast summers.
  4. Evaluate Operating Systems: Choose a manual lift or a motorized option. PowerView Automation is the Hunter Douglas app and smart-home system, and it can be scheduled so shades lower at set times. SoftTouch Motorization is a push-button wand, not an app or a voice system.
  5. Match Aesthetic Preferences: Duette shades come in a range of colors and textures to suit your interior. With Duolite, the light-filtering shade stays visible during the day, so its color and texture matter as much as the room-darkening layer behind it.

Overview

This guide explains how to take a custom window measurement for the most common window treatments, including blinds, shades, shutters, and drapery. It covers inside versus outside mount, obstructions, bay and corner windows, and the tolerance you should expect.

Inside Versus Outside Mount

The first decision in any custom window measurement is whether the treatment will sit inside the window opening or mount on the wall or trim around it. Inside mount provides a clean, built-in appearance and is suitable when the window has sufficient depth for the headrail. Outside mount covers more of the wall and is ideal for shallow openings, maximum light control, or when obstructions prevent a recessed fit.

For an inside mount, measure the width and height of the window opening in three places: top, middle, and bottom for width, and left, center, and right for height. Use the smallest width and the largest height, because windows are rarely perfectly square. For an outside mount, measure the width and height of the area you want the treatment to cover, then add overlap on each side and above the opening so the treatment blocks light and provides privacy.

Mount Type What to Measure Best For
Inside Mount The window opening, at three points for width and three for height. A clean, recessed look when the window has adequate depth.
Outside Mount The area to be covered, plus overlap on the sides and top. Shallow windows, maximum light control, and obstructions.

Accounting for Obstructions

Handles, cranks, and window hardware can change the measurement you need. Note the location and how far each obstruction projects from the window, because that projection determines the clearance or stand-off your chosen treatment requires. A crank that sticks out into the opening may rule out a flush inside mount, while a handle on a door can interfere with a shade that lowers too close to the frame.

Trim and molding matter too. If the window has decorative trim, decide whether the treatment will cover it or sit within it, and measure accordingly. For outside mounts, the mounting surface may be the wall, the trim, or a combination, so confirm where the brackets will attach before you finalize the width. Getting these details right at the measurement stage avoids gaps, rubbing, and operation problems after installation.

Bay and Corner Windows

Bay and corner windows are measured one section at a time. Each pane has its own width and height, and the angles where the sections meet affect how the treatments align. Measure every section individually rather than treating the bay as a single opening, and note the depth available at each section for mounting hardware.

For corner windows, plan how the treatments will meet at the corner so they do not collide when operated. Drapery, shades, and blinds each handle corners differently, and the measurement you take should reflect the product you plan to install. If the bay has a seat or a deep sill, measure the depth from the glass to the front edge so the treatment clears the sill and any furniture below.

Tolerance and Final Checks

Custom window treatments are made to your measurements, and a small tolerance is normal. A variation of roughly 1/8 to 1/4 inch is typical for blinds and shades, and the exact tolerance depends on the manufacturer and the product. That allowance lets the treatment fit and operate smoothly inside the opening instead of binding against the frame.

Before you order, double-check your numbers and confirm the mount type, the control side, and any special requirements such as cordless operation or motorization. If you are unsure about a measurement, a professional measure removes the guesswork. Why Professional Measurement Matters

A precise measurement protects the investment you make in custom window treatments. When the width, height, and depth are correct, the treatment fits the opening, the fabric or slats operate without rubbing, and the finished look matches the design you had in mind. When a measurement is off, even by a small amount, the result can be gaps at the edges, a shade that will not fully close, or hardware that does not sit flush.

Professional measurement also catches details that are easy to miss at home, such as out-of-square openings, uneven trim, and obstructions that affect clearance. Our team measures each window, confirms the mount type, and reviews the product options with you so the order is correct the first time. Whether you are updating one room or a whole home, accurate measurement is the foundation of a result you will be happy with for years.

How Duolite and LightLock Work Together

Duolite is not a separate shade line. It is a construction option on Hunter Douglas shades that puts two fabrics on one headrail: a room-darkening layer and a light-filtering or sheer layer. You raise or lower each layer independently, so the same window can be bright and open in the morning and much darker at night without swapping anything out.

LightLock is a side channel that runs along the vertical edges of select Hunter Douglas shades such as Duette. Standard shades leave a small gap on each side where light slips past the fabric. The LightLock channel covers those gaps, which is often the difference between a room that feels dim and one that feels genuinely dark.

Neither product is a blackout curtain, and neither turns a bedroom into a photographic darkroom. They reduce the light that comes through and around the shade. For most bedrooms on the Treasure Coast, that is exactly the goal.
